What a wedding planner takes off your plate

A wedding planner works for you. A venue coordinator works for the venue. That single difference explains most of the confusion couples run into, and it is worth being clear about before you decide whether you need to hire anyone at all.

Your venue coordinator handles what happens inside the venue and is usually included in your venue fee. What they do not do is find your photographer, chase your celebrant, manage your budget across twelve suppliers, tell you that your ceremony time will not leave enough light for photos, or stand at the gate at 7am directing a marquee crew. The wedding coordinators page sets the two roles out line by line if you want the full comparison.

A wedding planner does those things. They also carry the parts of a wedding that have nothing to do with the venue at all: the guest logistics, the family politics, the supplier who has gone quiet, and the decisions that need making in a particular order so that the later ones are still available to you.

Packages

Wedding planner packages, and what is in each one

Almost every Australian wedding planner sells three packages. The names change. The scope is remarkably consistent.

Full wedding planning

Your planner runs the wedding from the first conversation to the last song. This is the package to look at if you are planning from another city, working long hours, or your guest list is over 100.

Typically engaged nine to fourteen months out.

  • Concept, styling direction and colour
  • Venue shortlist, site visits and contract review
  • Every supplier sourced, quoted and booked
  • Budget held and tracked in one place
  • Full run sheet and on-the-day management

Partial wedding planning

You have the venue and the date. Your planner picks up the suppliers you have not booked, builds the timeline and takes over the jobs that keep sliding.

Usually engaged four to eight months out.

  • You keep the decisions you care about
  • Supplier shortlists and introductions
  • Timeline and budget management
  • Styling refined against what is already booked
  • Coordination on the day

On-the-day coordination

You plan the wedding. Someone else runs it. Your coordinator takes the plan four to six weeks out and becomes the contact for everyone.

Usually engaged two to three months out.

  • Your plan and suppliers stay exactly as they are
  • Handover meeting four to six weeks before
  • Every supplier confirmed and briefed
  • Run sheet written and circulated
  • On-site management for the whole day

More on on-the-day coordination

Cost

How much does a wedding planner cost in Australia?

Two of the most cited Australian sources give different answers, and the gap is worth understanding before you read any planner's quote.

Easy Weddings, in a guide updated in February 2026 and drawing on its 2025 Wedding Industry Report, puts full-service wedding planning at $5,000 to $6,000, a day-of coordinator at roughly $1,500 to $2,000, and hourly consultations at $75 to $100. It notes that a $6,000 planning fee is around 17 per cent of the average Australian wedding budget of $35,315.

Airtasker's Australian wedding planner cost guide, updated February 2025, gives a much wider $1,000 to $20,000 range with a median around $8,000, quotes hourly rates of $70 to $120, and observes that planners commonly charge 10 to 15 per cent of the total wedding budget rather than a flat fee. It also estimates that planning a single wedding takes 200 to 300 hours.

Both are describing a real market. They diverge because they are measuring different scopes. Flat fee quotes cluster where Easy Weddings sits. Percentage quotes rise with your budget, so on a $90,000 wedding a 12 per cent fee lands near $11,000 and looks nothing like the flat-fee figure. Wedding planner prices are a function of scope and budget, not a fixed rate card.

When you compare wedding planner cost between two quotes, compare the scope first. A quote that looks $3,000 cheaper is often a partial planning package sitting next to a full planning one.

200 to 300

10 to 15%

Timing

How far ahead do wedding planners get booked?

01

Twelve to eighteen months out

If you want full planning, this is the window. Planners take a limited number of weddings per season and the good ones fill peak Saturdays first.

02

Six to nine months out

The usual partial planning window. The venue is booked, a few suppliers are locked in, and the middle of the list has stopped moving.

03

Two to three months out

On-the-day coordination. Late enough that your plan is real, early enough for a coordinator to learn it properly before the handover.

04

Under six weeks

Still possible, but your options narrow sharply and some coordinators will decline on the basis that they cannot do the handover properly.

Further afield

Destination and interstate weddings

A destination wedding planner is worth more than a local one, not less. When you cannot do site visits, cannot meet suppliers, and do not know which streets flood in February, you are buying local knowledge you have no other way of getting.

There are two models. Some couples engage a planner based in the destination, who knows the venues and suppliers first hand. Others engage a planner from home who travels, which keeps the relationship close but adds travel and accommodation to the fee, and means the supplier network is built rather than inherited. Both work. Ask which one you are being quoted.

For interstate weddings inside Australia, the same logic applies at a smaller scale. A Sydney planner running a Hunter Valley wedding is normal. A Sydney planner running a Margaret River wedding is a travel conversation.

Ask about the travel line

Travel, accommodation and extra site visits are the three things most likely to be excluded from a headline fee for a wedding outside a planner's usual area. Get them itemised before you sign.

Straight answers

Wedding planner questions

How much does a wedding planner cost?

Published Australian ranges differ by thousands. Easy Weddings, updated February 2026, quotes $5,000 to $6,000 for full-service planning and around $1,500 to $2,000 for a day-of coordinator. Airtasker's Australian guide gives $1,000 to $20,000 with a median near $8,000 and notes a common 10 to 15 per cent of budget model. The variable is scope. Compare package inclusions before you compare wedding planner prices.

Do I need a wedding planner if my venue has a coordinator?

They do different jobs. A venue coordinator manages what happens inside the venue and works for the venue. A wedding planner works for you and manages everything outside it, including supplier sourcing, budget and the overall timeline. Many couples with a venue coordinator still hire an on-the-day coordinator for exactly this reason.

What is partial wedding planning?

Partial wedding planning is for couples who have booked the venue and some suppliers and want a planner to take the rest. It typically covers supplier shortlisting for what is left, timeline and budget management, styling refinement and coordination on the day. It sits between full planning and on-the-day coordination in both scope and price.

Can I hire a wedding planner for a destination wedding?

Yes, and it is one of the strongest cases for hiring one. A destination wedding planner either lives in the destination and brings local supplier knowledge, or travels from home with travel costs added. Ask which model you are being quoted, because it changes both the fee and what the planner actually knows.

Does a wedding planner have to be local to me?

No. Typing wedding planner near me will show you businesses close to you, but Australian planners work to a service area rather than a shopfront, and most cover a whole metropolitan region plus the country around it. What matters is whether they have worked at your venue or at venues like it, and what they charge to travel. For a regional wedding, travel and accommodation should be itemised in the quote.

What does a luxury wedding planner do differently?

Usually three things: fewer weddings per season, a larger on-site team, and access to suppliers who work by referral. The planning process itself is the same. Where the fee rises sharply is in production scope, such as custom build, imported florals or multi-day programmes, rather than in the planning work itself.

When should I hire a wedding planner?

For full planning, nine to fourteen months before the wedding is the usual window in Australia. Partial planning tends to start six to nine months out and on-the-day coordination two to three months out. Enquiring earlier costs nothing and gives you more planners to choose from, particularly for a Saturday in spring or autumn.
